- When sentiment is negative (especially > -0.5) and forecast is trending up, reduce forecast by 1–2% to avoid overcorrection.  
- If recent history shows strong upward momentum (e.g., 3+ consecutive price increases) and sentiment is neutral or slightly positive, model tends to overestimate — cap forecast peak at 10–15% below true high.  
- If forecast spikes sharply after a dip (e.g., 3–5 days of low prices), reduce the spike by 5–10% to avoid overshoot.  
- When sentiment is positive and forecast is flat or slightly down, increase forecast by 1–3% to capture sentiment-driven momentum.  
- If true outcome consistently exceeds forecast by 2–5% over 3–5 days, apply a 1–2% upward bias correction for next period.  
- If sentiment is consistently negative and forecast is trending down, avoid premature correction — allow 1–2 days of lag before adjusting downward.  
- For 30-day horizon, if forecast mean is 1–2% below true mean, apply a 1–2% upward adjustment to align with sentiment-driven mean reversion.
